title: Ants stop eating the soil -- and stack what they dig out
question: The spoil holds itself up, so a colony builds it into that lattice reaching out from the bank. Live with it, or should the spoil fall and pile even though that closes the tunnels?
context_md:
Your report: digging consumed the soil and a bed ran down to nothing. It does not any more -- an ant comes away from the face with a lump of ground in its jaws, cannot cut anything else while it is holding one, and puts it back down wherever its own drop impulse fires. **Nothing left the world in B.** The same bank, the same seed, 8,000 frames.

Where it puts them is the ants' decision, not a rule I wrote (two rules I wrote are in the record as failures). What I could not decide by measurement is what you are looking at:

- **A lump an ant puts down is *tamped*, the way it tamps a tunnel wall.** Tamped ground holds itself up. So a pellet can be set down on top of an earlier pellet, and over seven hundred of them a colony grows the scaffold you can see in B, out into open air.
- **Loose spoil instead falls and piles like any dirt -- and closes the tunnels.** Measured both ways: standing tunnel void went from 54-58 cells tamped to **2-3** loose. That is the whole nest, gone.

So it is a real fork and I do not think either side is obviously right.

Also worth knowing, and reported rather than tuned: **B's nest is smaller.** Tunnel void 39 against 89 here, at nearly three times the digging, because an ant that lets go underground fills in what it just cut. That is the ant's `drop` gene, so it is something a colony could get better at rather than something fixed in the engine.

items.label: A -- today: the spoil is destroyed
items.caption: the bank is eaten away; nothing is put back

items.label: B -- the ants carry it out
items.caption: every cell dug is put back somewhere -- including out in the air
